books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom”

stimulus.text:
“The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line,—the relation of the darker to the lighter races of men in Asia and Africa, in America and the islands of the sea. It was a phase of this problem that caused the Civil War; and however much they who marched South and North in 1861 may have fixed on the technical points, of union and local autonomy as a shibboleth, all nevertheless knew, as we know, that the question of Negro slavery was the real cause of the conflict.”

—W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom”
stimulus.source_note: W. E. B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903), Chapter 2, “Of the Dawn of Freedom.” Public domain (Project Gutenberg eBook #408). Wording verified against the Gutenberg text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Du Bois opens his chapter on Reconstruction’s aftermath with the “color-line.” His point is that

options.text: the Civil War had settled the question of race in America.
options.misconception: Du Bois says the color-line is the problem of the new century, unsettled, not settled.

options.text: slavery was a minor cause of the Civil War.
options.misconception: Du Bois says the opposite: slavery was “the real cause of the conflict.”

options.text: the racial struggle behind the war would define the century that followed.
Reconstruction had solved the problems of the freedpeople.
options.misconception: The whole chapter measures Reconstruction’s failures; Du Bois opens with the problem still unsolved.

rationales.A: Du Bois says the color-line is the problem of the new century, unsettled, not settled.
rationales.B: Du Bois says the opposite: slavery was “the real cause of the conflict.”
rationales.C: Du Bois looks back at the war and forward to the century ahead, and sees one line running through both: the color-line. The war was one phase of it, and the unfinished work of Reconstruction would be the next.
rationales.D: The whole chapter measures Reconstruction’s failures; Du Bois opens with the problem still unsolved.
rationales.general:
1. Du Bois names the new century’s problem in his first line: the color-line.
2. He then ties it backward: a phase of this same problem caused the Civil War.
3. The war’s fighters talked of union and local autonomy, but all knew slavery was the real cause.
4. So the line did not end at Appomattox; it ran on into the century Du Bois was writing in.
Remember: a writer’s opening line is often the whole argument in miniature.
